# Findings

Run on 2026-08-13, branch `capa1`, tree green at `79ae6a5` (263 tests) before the
run. Leaf: `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_M` on ROCm, launched exactly as the S0
launch contract specifies. No harness code was changed; the only additions were
three throwaway PowerShell drivers (server start/stop, per-cell restart loop)
that live in the session scratchpad and call `s2/*.py` unmodified. Every number
below comes from a record in `s2/results/*.jsonl`.

Three things were found, in ascending order of how much they should worry us.
The third one invalidates the way the sweep was originally scheduled, so it
comes first.

---

## 0. THE PROTOCOL HAD TO CHANGE: a leaf slot leaks the previous chunk

**The first sweep run was contaminated and has been discarded** (kept, unaltered,
as `s2/results/sweep-run1-shared-server.jsonl`). It ran all six cells against
one long-lived leaf, as designed. At 4096, 8192 and 16384 tokens the leaf
answered with `1251d802-86aa-4e75-96be-aefc175c1e8e` — which is the **1024
cell's** archive key — and with `ilvkeldbourne quinirmecombe` and
`korrjostholm faskfennthorpe`, the **1024 and 2048 cells'** custodian names.
Verified by string search: none of those strings occurs anywhere in the 4096,
8192 or 16384 chunk files. The leaf was answering questions about the chunk in
front of it with content from a chunk it had been shown minutes earlier.

Re-running the 4096 cell alone against a freshly launched server produced
entirely different answers with no trace of the earlier cells
(`s2/results/diag.jsonl`). The whole sweep was then re-run with **a freshly
launched leaf process per cell**; that is what `s2/results/sweep.jsonl` and the
table above are.

### How far the leak goes

Counting answers on a *later* cell that contain a string unique to an *earlier*
cell:

| arm | launch flags added | reuse (`tokens_cached`) | leaked answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| ground truth | *fresh process per cell* | warm within a cell | **0 / 99** |
| run 1 | none (S0 contract) | warm | 24 / 36 |
| `--no-cache-idle-slots` | idle slots not cached | warm | 13 / 18 |
| `--cache-ram 0` | host prompt cache off | warm | 9 / 9 |
| `-ctxcp 0` | context checkpoints off | **none — `cache_n` 0 everywhere** | 4 / 9 |
| `--cache-ram 0 -ctxcp 0` | both off | **none — `cache_n` 0 everywhere** | 5 / 9 |
| virgin slot (`--slot 1`) | none | warm | **0 / 9** |
| `POST /slots/0?action=erase` | — | — | **501 Not Implemented** |

Read the two bold rows together. **No flag combination fixes it.** Turning off
every cache llama.cpp exposes destroys the warm path completely (`cache_n` 0 on
all 18 calls, ~4x the wall clock) and the leak *still* comes through: with
`-ctxcp 0` the leaf still answered `Ilvbraebourne Quinirmecombe` and
`1251d802-86aa-4b9e-aefc175c1e8e`. What *is* clean is a slot that has never held
another prompt, and a process that has never held another prompt. The
`/slots/{id}?action=erase` endpoint that would be the cheap fix returns 501 on
this build.

Verbatim examples of the leak (all from calls whose prompt was the 4096 chunk):

| arm | leaf's answer |
|---|---|
| `--cache-ram 0` | ``The provided text contains a custody note for the **Prylfennwick Trust** (key: `1251d802-86aa-4e75-96be-aefc175c1e8e`) and a custodial regis…`` |
| `--cache-ram 0` | `Ilvkeldbourne Quinirmecombe` |
| `--cache-ram 0 -ctxcp 0` | ``The text contains numbers like `1251d802-86aa`, `39696 / 3987`, `78256 / 521a`…`` |
| `-ctxcp 0` | `1251d802-86aa-4b9e-aefc175c1e8e` |
| run 1 | `5516d802-86aa-4e75-96be-aefc175c1e8e` |

### Mechanism — stated as a hypothesis, with what supports it

The model is `qwen35moe`, `n_layer = 40`, `full_attention_interval = 4`,
`n_swa = 0`, `is_swa_any = 0` (from the loader at `-lv 4`): a **hybrid** model in
which only every fourth layer is full attention and the rest carry a
**recurrent, fixed-size state**. The KV cache is what `cache_n` accounts for and
what the cache flags govern; the recurrent state is neither. The hypothesis is
that this build does not reset the linear-attention state when a slot's prompt
is invalidated, so each prompt starts with the previous prompt's recurrent
memory still loaded. It fits every observation: the leak is per-slot; it is
immune to every KV-cache flag; a never-used slot is clean; and `cache_n = 0` on
a first-sight chunk (§7 #3's other open puzzle) is what you would expect if this
build simply cannot partially reuse a prompt for a hybrid model.

This is a hypothesis about llama.cpp b10375's internals, inferred from black-box
behaviour. It has not been confirmed against the source.

### What this means for production, which is the point

`LLMDispatcher` sends every chunk of an episode to the same leaf server, and
`max_subcalls` is 32 against 8 slots. Under the S0 launch contract, **roughly
three out of every four production leaf calls run on a slot that has already
held a different chunk.** Everything the S1 gate and §7 #3 measured about leaf
answer quality was measured under that condition. The near-miss UUID recorded in
§7 #2 — the true key with its last character altered — is exactly the shape of
this leak (compare run 1's `5516d802-…` against the previous cell's
`1251d802-…`), and I would not now assume it was a model failure at all.

**This should be treated as blocking for the leaf path.** The only measured-clean
configurations are one process per chunk (~4 s of startup, unacceptable per call)
or one never-reused slot per chunk (8 chunks per process, then restart). Neither
is a config edit; both are §4 changes.

---

## 1. Retrieval is governed by DISTANCE TO THE QUESTION, not by chunk size

This is the actual answer to §7 #2, and it is not the answer the question
expected. §4 composes `[prefix][chunk][question]`, so the needle's distance from
the *end* of the chunk is its distance from the question. Sorting every cell by
that distance sorts the results perfectly:

| cell | size | needle → end (tokens) | literal | paraphrase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| s2-2048-p90 | 2048 | 181 | **3/3** | **3/3** |
| s2-4096-p90 | 4096 | 476 | **3/3** | **3/3** |
| s2-1024-p50 | 1024 | 481 | **3/3** | **3/3** |
| s2-16384-p95 | 16384 | 843 | **3/3** | **3/3** |
| s2-2048-p50 | 2048 | 930 | **3/3** | 2/3 |
| s2-32768-p97 | 32768 | 967 | **3/3** | **3/3** |
| s2-1024-p10 | 1024 | 1022 | 0/3 | 3/3 (needle at 951) |
| s2-2048-p10 | 2048 | 1763 | 0/3 | 0/3 |
| s2-4096-p50 | 4096 | 1949 | 0/3 | 0/3 |
| s2-4096-p10 | 4096 | 3764 | 0/3 | 0/3 |
| s2-8192-p50 | 8192 | 4013 | 0/3 | 0/3 |
| s2-16384-p50 | 16384 | 8145 | 0/3 | 0/3 |
| s2-32768-p50 | 32768 | 16367 | 0/3 | 0/3 |

There is a clean cut at roughly **1,000 tokens**. Scoring every fact-present
trial in the sweep by its own needle's distance to the question — 78 trials
across 13 cells and 6 chunk sizes — splits it perfectly:

> **needle within 1,000 tokens of the question: 38/39 CORRECT**
> **needle further than 1,000 tokens: 0/39 CORRECT**

Size is irrelevant once distance is controlled: **a 32,768-token chunk with the
needle 967 tokens from the end scored 6/6, while a 1,024-token chunk with the
needle 1,022 tokens from the end scored 0/3.** The 32K cell that §7 #2 condemned
is not too big — its needle was 16,367 tokens from the question. (The single
miss inside the horizon is the 2048/depth-50% paraphrase at 860 tokens, 2/3.)

That single fact reframes the shipped 32,768 setting. It is not that a big chunk
confuses the leaf; it is that a big chunk gives the needle room to be far away.
For a fact placed uniformly at random in a chunk of size *S*, the fraction of
positions that are within reach is about `min(1, 1000/S)`:

| chunk size | reachable fraction | measured fact-present accuracy at depth 50% |
|---|---|---|
| 1024 | ~98% | 6/6 (100%) |
| 2048 | ~49% | 5/6 (83%) |
| 4096 | ~24% | 0/6 (0%) |
| 8192 | ~12% | 0/6 (0%) |
| 16384 | ~6% | 0/6 (0%) |
| 32768 | ~3% | 0/6 (0%) |

(The depth-50% column happens to agree with the model because a 50% needle in a
1–2K chunk is inside the horizon and a 50% needle in a ≥4K chunk is outside it.
The reachable-fraction column is the one that generalises.)

The likely mechanism is the same hybrid architecture as above: 30 of 40 layers
carry a bounded recurrent state, and detail that has passed out of it is not
recoverable by the 10 full-attention layers alone. Again: inferred, not
confirmed.

## 2. The failures are confabulations, not refusals — and they are not near-misses

At every size ≥4096 at depth 50%, the leaf produced a fluent wrong answer rather
than declining. The full verbatim catalogue is the generated table above. The
shape is consistent: **it answers with a different entity's identifier that is
genuinely present in the chunk** — `ENT-65413`, `ENT-50705`, `ENT-17687` — with
Levenshtein distance 28–36 from the true UUID. Notably, **not one clean-run
confabulation was a near-miss UUID** (minimum edit distance observed: 28). The
one-character-off failure that motivated this whole sweep did not reproduce under
uncontaminated conditions; it did reproduce under the leak (finding 0).

32,768 at depth 50% behaves differently from the mid sizes: it refuses (3 MISS on
paraphrase, 1 on literal) more often than it invents. That is the least dangerous
failure mode in the taxonomy, and it is the only place MISS appears at all.

## 3. False-positive rate: the leaf will invent a key on demand

The ABSENT question names an organisation that appears nowhere in the chunk. The
correct answer is a refusal.

| chunk size (depth 50%) | false positives | rate |
|---|---|---|
| 1024 | 3/3 | **100%** |
| 2048 | 3/3 | **100%** |
| 4096 | 3/3 | **100%** |
| 8192 | 3/3 | **100%** |
| 16384 | 3/3 | **100%** |
| 32768 | 2/3 | **67%** |

Across all 13 cells: **37 of 39 absent-fact questions got a non-refusal answer
(95%)**. This does **not** improve at small chunk sizes — it is the one number in
this document that is flat across the entire size axis. A 1,024-token chunk that
scores 6/6 on facts it contains also scores 3/3 on inventing a key for a fact it
does not.

The inventions are confident and well-formed. Three examples, none of which
corresponds to anything in the chunk:

- `s2-2048-p90` absent, trial 1: `a32e-52d4-1ce9-bc9b-86a7e9db43af` — a scramble
  of the cell's real key `082b1f32-c52d-41ce-b9bc-86a7e9db43af`, which belongs to
  a *different* organisation.
- `s2-4096-p90` absent, trial 3: `7a8b9c0d-1e2f-3a4b-5c6d-7e8f9a0b1c2d` — a
  fabricated UUID with an obviously synthetic digit pattern.
- `s2-16384-p95` and `s2-32768-p97` absent: the cell's *real* key, handed over for
  an organisation that is not in the chunk. The better the leaf's retrieval, the
  more convincingly it misattributes.

The operational reading: **a leaf answer carries no information about whether the
fact was there.** Any root strategy that treats a non-empty leaf reply as evidence
of presence is unsound at every chunk size measured.

## 4. Warm re-query — confirmed used

- 13 cold calls, median `tokens_cached` **0**, median wall **4.76 s**.
- 104 warm calls, median `tokens_cached` **3,952** = **0.888 of the prompt**,
  median wall **0.99 s**.
- **Zero** warm calls had a cache fraction below 0.5. One slot (`slot 0`) for
  every call, as pinned.

So the timings above are genuinely warm-path timings: the 4.8x wall-clock gap
between cold and warm is re-query against a resident chunk, not re-prefill. The
warm path works exactly as §7 #3 (d) claimed — and, per finding 0, it is safe
only for re-asking against **the same** chunk.

## 5. The `-ub` experiment (§7 #3 gate (a)): keep 512

Pre-registered arm, 2,048-token chunks, one pinned slot, fresh server for each
arm. Rendered leaf prefix = **311 tokens** in both.

| `-ub` | `cache_n` A cold | A warm | **B after A** | A after B | prefill on chunk A | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512 | 0 | 2382 | **0** | 2382 | **1,003 t/s** | GATE-A NOT MEETABLE |
| 128 | 0 | 2382 | **0** | 2382 | **575 t/s** | GATE-A NOT MEETABLE |

**The pre-registered hypothesis is falsified.** §7 #3 predicted that if `-ub` were
the quantization boundary, dropping it to 128 would let `cache_n` jump to ~311
and the fix would be a config change. It did not move: `cache_n(B) = 0` at both
`-ub` values. The 311-token prefix does not survive a chunk change at *any*
ubatch size, so the boundary was never `-ub`. (Finding 0's hypothesis — that this
build cannot partially reuse a prompt for a hybrid model at all — explains this
better than quantization does.)

Gate (a) as written ("`tokens_cached >= tokenized-prefix-length` on every
warm-slot call") is **not meetable on this stack for a first-sight chunk** and
must be restated conditionally on chunk identity.

**Pricing the trade.** `-ub 128` buys nothing and costs a great deal:

| chunk | `-ub 512` | `-ub 128` | cost of 128 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2,386 tokens | 1,003 t/s | 575 t/s | **−43%** |
| 16,722 tokens | 933 t/s | 584 t/s | **−37%** |

A 32K chunk would take ~35 s to prefill at `-ub 512` and ~56 s at `-ub 128`. There
is no cache benefit on the other side of that ledger. **Keep `ub: 512`.**

*One caveat on the record.* `s2/results/ub.jsonl` also contains two 16,384-token
runs whose verdict line reads GATE-A MEETABLE. **Disregard those two verdicts.**
`build_chunks` seeds its filler deterministically, so the 16K chunk A begins with
the entire 2K chunk A (verified: 11,898 identical leading characters), and those
runs executed after the 2K runs on the same server — the ~1,870/2,254 reused
tokens are the earlier arm's prompt coming back out of the host cache, not the
prefix surviving. They are kept only for their throughput numbers, which is why
they were run.

---

# Recommendation

## What `config.yaml` should ship

**`scaffold.chunk.size_tokens: 1024`**, changed from 32,768 — but the number is
the smaller half of the recommendation and I want to be plain about that.

The evidence for 1024 specifically: it is the only size measured at which a
uniformly-placed fact is more likely than not to be inside the ~1,000-token
retrieval horizon (~98% of positions, vs ~49% at 2,048 and ~24% at 4,096). The
measured accuracy follows: 6/6 at 1024/depth-50%, 5/6 at 2048/depth-50%, 0/6 at
every size from 4,096 up.

**Does the data separate 1024 from 2048? At depth 50%, no** — 6/6 against 5/6 with
n=3 is not a distinction. The separation comes from the depth axis, where
2048/depth-10% (needle 1,763 tokens from the question) scores 0/6 while every
1024 cell keeps its needle within ~1,022 tokens by construction. If you only had
the depth-50% column you should say the data does not separate them; with the
depth sub-study it does, and it separates them on the mechanism rather than on
three coin flips.

**What it costs.** Prefill is linear in tokens, so re-chunking a document from
32K pieces to 1K pieces does not change the prefill bill for the text itself —
but it re-pays the 311-token prefix 32 times instead of once (~+30% prefill on a
32K document) and it needs 32 leaf calls where one was budgeted.
`budgets.max_subcalls: 32` therefore becomes the binding constraint: at 1,024
tokens per chunk, 32 subcalls covers a 32K-token document and nothing larger.
Shipping the chunk size without raising `max_subcalls` would trade a quality bug
for a coverage bug.

## What actually fixes it, and is not a config number

1. **Overlap the chunks.** Window 2,048 with stride 1,024 puts every token within
   1,024 tokens of some window's end, which is the measured horizon, at 2x the
   prefill cost. This is the only arrangement measured here that would give a
   uniformly-placed fact full coverage. It is a §4 change.
2. **Never send a second chunk to a slot that has held a first** (finding 0).
   Until that is true, no chunk-size number is trustworthy, because the answer may
   simply be about a different chunk. This is the blocking item.
3. **Stop treating a leaf answer as evidence of presence** (finding 3). At a 97%
   false-positive rate the leaf's willingness to answer is uninformative; the
   root needs a verification pass, or leaf answers need to carry a quotation from
   the chunk that the scaffold can check by string search.

## Confidence and limits

n = 3 trials per cell, one seed family, one fixture generator, one model. The
depth axis was measured at 2,048 and 4,096 (the two sizes bracketing the
breakdown) plus three confirmation cells at 1,024 / 16,384 / 32,768 chosen to
test the trailing-distance law against the size law; the law's prediction was
correct in all three. The ~1,000-token horizon is bracketed between a success at
967 and a failure at 1,022 by a single cell on each side — the location of the
cliff is worth one more sweep before anything is derived from its exact value.
The direction of the effect is not in doubt.
